chunks: As for what al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from his brother al-Ḥasan, from Zurʿah, from Samāʿah, who said:

I asked him about what invalidates wudu (ablution). He said: Hadath—when you hear its sound or find its smell—and rumbling in the belly, except for something you can restrain, or laughing during salat (prayer), and vomiting.

We have already spoken about this report previously, and we said that the proper way concerning it is to interpret it as referring to a condition in which a person has no control over himself, so that he knows what occurs from him; and it is also possible to understand it as indicating recommendation.

key_terms.الصَّلَاةِ: salat (prayer), in which laughing is mentioned
key_terms.الْحَدَثُ: ritual nullifying occurrence, here referring to what breaks wudu
key_terms.الْقَرْقَرَةُ: rumbling or gurgling in the belly
key_terms.الْوُضُوءَ: wudu (ablution), the ritual purification being discussed
key_terms.رِيحَهُ: its smell, used as a sign of passing wind

ai.seo_question: What does this hadith in al-Istibṣār say about what invalidates wudu (ablution)?
ai.summary: This hadith discusses matters said to invalidate wudu (ablution), especially the occurrence of hadath identified by sound or smell. The closing note explains that this report has already been addressed and may be understood either in a case where a person cannot control himself or as referring to recommendation rather than obligation.
